list.listitem: The most used amphetamines are MDMA (methylenedioxymethamphetamine, "Ecstasy," "Adam"), MDA (3,4-methylenedioxyamphetamine, tenamfetamine, "Eve"), and recently PMA (paramethoxyamphetamine). C

Amphetamine overdose can range from agitation and euphoria to hyperthermia and seizure, chest pain, acute coronary syndrome, and acute abdominal pain depending on the amphetamine, dose, and route of administration. Chronic amphetamine use may result in mild withdrawal symptoms lasting several days. A high level of suspicion of potential poisoning has to be maintained at the emergency department, especially for those young patients presenting with the symptoms and signs described above. C

Route of administration determines the rapidity of onset of clinical symptoms and signs as well as the duration, while severity may be dose-dependent. Onset of symptoms and signs is within minutes for intravenous and inhalational administration whereas there is a 1-hour delayed onset in oral use. For MDMA, onset of effects can take 20 to 60 minutes with peak effect occurring 60 to 90 minutes after ingestion and primary effects lasting 3 to 5 hours. Elimination half-life is 6 to 12 hours. C

Care in the acute setting includes maintaining ABC (Airway, Breathing and Circulation), supportive care including adequate sedation in a quiet environment, effective cooling in hyperthermia, close monitoring to evaluate for and manage as appropriate, end-organ toxicity and morbidity. There is no specific antidote for amphetamine overdose. C
Many patients may be stable enough for discharge after a short stay in the ED. C

Consider ICU admission for continued supportive care and close monitoring in patients with persistent symptoms several hours after intoxication, those comatose with evidence of end-organ dysfunction, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, or who continue to exhibit bizarre behavior and need further diagnostic work-up. C

Treatment of end-organ toxicity (e.g., cardiomyopathy, myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, arrhythmias; neurotoxicity as in stroke, seizures or persistent psychosis) will involve specialty referral and follow up. C
Amphetamines are notable for their influence on mood, arousal, increased energy and anorexia. Their physiological effects become toxic at escalating doses or with increased frequency of use.
About 39,000 drug abuse related ED visits involving amphetamines in 2002. A 54% increase was observed between 1995 and 2002 especially in metropolitan areas in Midwest, South and Northeast USA.
In a study of acute drug toxicity presentations to emergency rooms in 10 European countries, amphetamines were the 5th most common drug reported (behind heroin, cocaine, cannabis, and GHB/GBL).
In 2002, 65% of patients evaluated in an emergency department for amphetamine overdose were white and 58% were male; more than half were aged 18 to 34 years. Ethnic minority constituted about 17%.
About 30% of ED visits were attributed to overdose while 24% were the result of an unexpected reaction.

A database study of 340,000 U.S. persons aged 13 to 25 years who were newly prescribed an amphetamine or methylphenidate for ADHD found a slightly higher risk of psychosis in patients taking amphetamines (0.21% vs 0.1%, NNH=909).

A prospective study that followed patients through a mean age of 25 years did not find a higher or lower risk of subsequent substance use (e.g., marijuana, tobacco, heavy alcohol, and other substances) among children with ADHD who were treated with stimulants. Self-reported substance use (at least once) through adolescence and early adulthood occurred in 81.3% of study participants.

In a systematic review of the literature, based on the best quality evidence, small but significant deficits were identified for ecstasy users compared to controls in areas of attention, memory, psychomotor speed, executive systems functioning, and self-reported depressive symptoms.
Amphetamines increase release and prevent the breakdown of the neurotransmitters dopamine and norepinephrine and, to a lesser extent, serotonin.
High levels of these neurotransmitters cause agitation, hallucination, euphoria, delusions, abnormal movements and, in some cases, seizure.
The autonomic nervous system is frequently affected, causing tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, tremor, and, in some cases, hyperthermia.

The cardiovascular response to methamphetamine appears to differ by gender and concomitant drug use; in one study, women had larger peak change in diastolic BP following methamphetamine administration while for men, baseline heart rate and blood pressure were strong predictors of cardiovascular response following administration. Lifetime use and recent use of methamphetamine and nicotine did not predict cardiovascular response but recent alcohol use was associated with increased peak change in diastolic BP and current cannabis use was negatively correlated with peak HR change.
The increased muscle activity can lead to rhabdomyolysis and resulting decrease in renal function.

Suspect amphetamine toxicity in patients with complaints of chest pain, palpitations, diaphoresis, euphoria, fever, headaches, tremor, restlessness, insomnia, stroke, movement disorder, agitation and seizures.
Other symptoms include dysphoria, depression, exacerbation of motor and phonic tics, skin rash, hearing loss, fatigue, dyspnea on exertion and dependent edema.
Obtain history of amphetamine use, including timing, quantity, and route of administration. The history may need to come from a family member or friend if the patient exhibits altered mental status.
In patients with altered mental status brought in by EMS, prehospital assessment of vital signs, mental status, findings of pill bottles, needles and syringes and other tell-tale signs are important.

Physical examination should include trauma survey on AIS (Abbreviated Injury Scale), which rates injury by region and severity. In amphetamine toxicity, this injury is usually in the head and neck region and ranges from minor to fatal.

Findings on examination may include respiratory distress, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, high grade fever, choreoathetosis, disorientation, dysrhythmia which may require defibrillation, coma, agitation, seizures, focal neurologic deficits, skin rash, needle marks on skin. Fatal poisoning is usually preceded by convulsion and coma.
Individual patient's response to amphetamine varies widely and may not be dose-dependent as toxic symptoms may occur idiosyncratically at low doses.
Order serum glucose and electrolytes in patients with seizures or altered mental status. If no metabolic cause, consider CT scan of the head and EEG.

Obtain 12-lead ECG and cardiac enzymes in those with chest pain, hypertension, tachycardia or respiratory distress. ECG may show T-wave changes and new onset left bundle branch block. Cardiac enzymes may show elevated CK and CK-MB. These may result in non Q-wave myocardial infarction. Pulse oximetry or ABG and chest x-ray are indicated.
If amphetamine toxicity is suspected, check urine and serum toxicology. Urine may show amphetamines and methamphetamine for up to 12 hours after presentation.
With significant or prolonged hyperthermia, rule out infective causes.
Check creatinine kinase and urinalysis with microscopy to rule out rhabdomyolysis.

Generalized vasculitis in the small arteries can occur in long-term users of amphetamines. This can cause neurological complications like cerebral hemorrhage and infarction which may also occur form arterial hypertension resulting in stroke with neurological deficits.
Renal failure secondary to renal vasculitis has been described, which may be complicated by rhabdomyolysis.

Hepatotoxicity is a complication of amphetamine use. It can range from mild hepatitis to liver failure requiring liver transplant. The metabolic pathway of amphetamines (demethylation) involves cytochrome P450, especially CYP2D6 isoenzyme. Oxidative radicals produced in these pathways are normally reduced by glutathione which is rapidly depleted by amphetamine overdose. Excess of these radicals can cause cell necrosis. Spontaneous recovery is the norm, but in chronic users permanent damage to hepatocytes can occur.

Central hyperthermia is a potentially life-threatening effect of amphetamine toxicity. This probably occurs from hyperactivity, warm environment, muscle rigidity, seizures, and a central thermoregulatory effect. Hyperthermia can cause or aggravate end organ toxicity, DIC, and or rhabdomyolysis.
Do not give ipecac, charcoal, or begin gastric lavage without first consulting a poison center. Research has not shown better outcomes in the treatment of amphetamine overdose.
Supportive care is the mainstay of management in an acute setting. Evaluate and support airway, breathing, and circulation as needed.

Management of acute amphetamine poisoning is largely symptomatic and depends on route of administration and time lag. In oral ingestion if short time lag, gastric lavage and administration of activated charcoal is appropriate. Acidification of urine will hasten clearance and renal elimination of amphetamine. Whole bowel irrigation is indicated in suspected cases of body stuffing or packing.
Agitation and persisting seizures require titration of benzodiazepines and a calm soothing environment.
Hypertension and tachycardia can initially be managed with a benzodiazepine. In refractory cases with significant end-organ toxicity, IV phentolamine, nitroprusside or nitroglycerine should be used.

Haloperidol or droperidol or olanzapine can be used in management of patients who present with acute agitation, violence and psychosis. Droperidol produces a more rapid and profound sedation than lorazepam for methamphetamine toxicity.
Significant cardiac dysrhythmia may require cardioversion or defibrillation.

Hyperthermia should be treated with aggressive cooling with ice packs to groin and axilla. If hyperthermia and agitation are severe, patient may require neuromuscular paralysis to rapidly decrease temperature.

Haloperidol in combination with benzodiazepines can control agitation and movement disorder. Haloperidol alone should be avoided in patients at increased risk for seizures as it lowers seizure threshold.
Generous IV fluids can prevent rhabdomyolysis.

A randomized placebo controlled trial evaluated the combination of naltrexone 380 mg extended release injection every 3 weeks plus oral bupropion 450 mg/day and found a small but significant increase in the likelihood of a clinical response, defined as 3 of 4 urine samples negative (13.6% vs 2.5%, p < 0.001, NNT = 9).
Patient education on the toxic effects of amphetamines should be done at discharge and follow-up visits.
Patients with persistent toxic psychosis may benefit from referral to outpatient detoxification program.
Generally prognosis is fair; patients without end organ toxicity may be fit for discharge after clinical stabilization in the ED.
Some effects of toxicity are transient and reversible (e.g. hearing loss).

Patient may require admission for monitoring and treatment for severe sequela of acute or chronic amphetamine toxicity. Close hospital discharge follow up is needed to manage end organ toxicity or damage.
Patients with cardiotoxicity presenting with acute MI, CHF, or arrhythmias will need cardiology consult and follow up.
